reference.source: Primer on the Metabolic Bone Diseases and Disorders of Mineral Metabolism (ASBMR)
clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive sclerosing dysplasia caused by a deletion of a downstream regulatory (enhancer) element that controls SOST expression, reducing sclerostin production
Closely related to sclerosteosis but generally milder, and importantly it lacks the syndactyly and overgrowth of stature seen in sclerosteosis
Reduced sclerostin releases the brake on Wnt-mediated bone formation, producing generalised osteosclerosis with prominent mandibular enlargement
Cranial and skull-base thickening entraps cranial nerves, causing facial palsy, hearing loss, and sometimes optic compromise
Patients typically have raised alkaline phosphatase reflecting increased bone formation, with normal calcium and phosphate
Radiographs show endosteal cortical thickening of long bones and dense sclerotic skull and jaw
Care centres on surgical decompression of entrapped nerves and surveillance for raised intracranial pressure rather than pharmacological bone reduction
reference.pathophysiology: Van Buchem disease is caused by homozygous deletion of a conserved regulatory region located downstream of the SOST gene. This element normally drives SOST transcription in bone, so its loss markedly reduces sclerostin expression while leaving the coding sequence intact. Diminished sclerostin fails to inhibit the Wnt/beta-catenin pathway, resulting in increased osteoblastic bone formation and progressive generalised hyperostosis. Because sclerostin is reduced rather than completely absent as in coding-mutation sclerosteosis, the phenotype is usually less severe, but skull and jaw overgrowth still narrows cranial foramina and can compress cranial nerves.
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs showing endosteal cortical thickening and dense skull and mandible
Serum alkaline phosphatase and bone turnover markers
Serum calcium and phosphate to confirm normal mineral homeostasis
Genetic testing for the SOST regulatory-region deletion
Skull-base imaging for foraminal narrowing and nerve compression
Audiology and visual assessment with monitoring for raised intracranial pressure
redFlags: Progressive facial-nerve weakness or deteriorating hearing or vision
Brainstem compression from posterior skull-base overgrowth
Acute neurological decline requiring urgent surgical decompression
reference.prognosis: Generally milder and more indolent than sclerosteosis, with a normal lifespan in most patients, but progressive cranial nerve entrapment can cause facial palsy and sensory loss that may require surgical relief.
pitfalls: Assuming a coding SOST mutation when the underlying lesion is a regulatory-region deletion
Confusing it with sclerosteosis and expecting syndactyly or gigantism, which are absent here
Overlooking treatable cranial nerve entrapment presenting as isolated facial palsy or deafness
Failing to monitor for raised intracranial pressure over time

management: No disease-specific pharmacotherapy; management centres on surveillance and surgical relief of complications
Surgical decompression of narrowed cranial foramina to relieve facial nerve, auditory or optic nerve entrapment
Audiological monitoring with hearing rehabilitation and hearing aids for hearing loss
Ophthalmic surveillance and management of optic nerve compromise and raised intracranial pressure
Serial skull-base and long-bone imaging to detect progressive hyperostosis and foraminal narrowing
Biochemical monitoring of alkaline phosphatase with confirmation of normal calcium and phosphate
Autosomal recessive genetic counselling and cascade family screening
